Note::TexAccessor::math_only¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::TexAccessor::math_only() const

Project Each Cell Onto Its Authored Formulae¶

math_only() removes prose and joins the contents of every complete math region in a Text cell. It recognizes $...$, $$...$$, \(...\), and \[...\], strips those outer delimiters, trims each recovered body, and joins non-empty bodies with one ASCII space. The result is useful when formula text, rather than its inline/display layout, is the material to index or transform.

This method is a shape-preserving projection, not a ragged extractor. One input cell always produces one output cell. A cell with no complete non-empty math region becomes the empty string, which preserves its location in a matrix or higher-rank Note. Use math_blocks when every region must remain a separate token with its original delimiters and per-cell offsets.

Delimiter recognition is shared with the math extractors. An escaped dollar is literal content, $$ is recognized before $, a single-dollar region cannot cross a physical newline, and unmatched openers are ignored. Commands and spacing inside a recovered body are otherwise retained; math_only() does not evaluate TeX, expand macros, or validate a formula. Joining normalizes whitespace between regions and trims the final cell, but does not remove commands from inside a region.

The receiver is not mutated. A new Text Note with the same rank and shape is allocated, including for scalar and empty-shaped inputs. Undefined input stays undefined, and every defined non-Text dtype is rejected before transformation. The kernel scans each source cell linearly and copies only retained formula bodies into the result arena.

Example 1: Project All Four Delimiter Forms¶

const auto source = pluss::make_note(
    std::vector<std::string>{
        R"(price \$5, $x+\$y$, $$z$$, and \(q\))",
        "\\[a+b\\] then $line\nbreak$", R"(\(unfinished)", "plain"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 2});

std::cout << source.tex().math_only() << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["x+\\$y z q", "a+b"],
  ["", ""]
]

The escaped currency dollar is not an opener, while the escaped dollar inside the first formula remains content. The newline prevents the second cell’s single-dollar candidate from becoming a region. Unmatched and math-free cells remain present as empty strings.

Example 2: Contrast Projection With Extraction¶

const auto projected = source.tex().math_only();
const auto extracted = source.tex().math_blocks(-1);

std::cout << "projected shape=[" << projected.sizes()[0] << ", "
          << projected.sizes()[1] << "]\n";
std::cout << extracted.tokens() << '\n';

Output¶

projected shape=[2, 2]
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["$x+\\$y$", "$$z$$", "\\(q\\)", "\\[a+b\\]"]

Projection keeps one lane per source cell; extraction keeps one lane per match.

Example 3: Undefined And Invalid Input¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << pluss::Note::undefined().tex().math_only().defined() << '\n';
try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2})
      .tex().math_only();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "math only Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

false
math only Int64: rejected
